cf.title: pgstat: Flush some statistics within running transactions, take 2

input.subject: pgstat: Flush some statistics within running transactions, take 2

verdict_reasoning: No surviving objection is fatal, and none is at level 1. Two fixable level 2 points remain. replication-ondisk-1: a custom stats callback ported with the smallest change double counts without any error. standards-compat-2: the existing pg_stat_force_next_flush() takes on immediate-flush behaviour under a name that says "next". A committer who knows pgstat has to decide both; neither stops the idea.

brief.title: Make pg_stat_force_next_flush() flush statistics inside a running transaction
brief.problem: A backend publishes its pending statistics only at transaction end, so a long transaction stays invisible in the cumulative statistics views until it commits or aborts. The author needs an on-demand mid-transaction flush for extensions, first for planned pg_stat_statements scalability work, and for users and tests that want current numbers.
brief.proposed_design: pg_stat_force_next_flush() flushes immediately when called in a transaction, and a C API does the same for the calling backend. Non-transactional counters such as scans and blocks hit are flushed at once, while tuple insert, update and delete counters wait for the transaction boundary. Pending entries stay allocated until transaction end with a flushed baseline, so each flush publishes only the delta, and entries that receive new counters during a pass are requeued.
user_visible_surface: pg_stat_force_next_flush() flushes immediately inside a transaction, becomes PARALLEL UNSAFE, and is now documented (catversion bump).
last_seq_scan and last_idx_scan use the statement start time when flushed during a transaction.
flush_pending_cb takes a new xact_boundary argument and returns a PgStat_FlushResult enum (LOCK_CONFLICT, DONE, PARTIAL) instead of bool.
Custom stats callbacks must not merge retained pending data twice and must not call pgstat_force_next_flush().
author_claims: Only callers that force a flush mid-transaction pay any cost, and an unchanged retained entry costs a memcmp, not a lock.
A benchmark with up to 512 relations and 256 clients showed no difference beyond about 1% tps noise for the per-pass reset scan.
Throttling belongs to the caller, so pgstat needs no rate limit.
The change is needed for the pg_stat_statements scalability patches in another thread.
brief.thread_state: Bertrand Drouvot reviewed many versions and called v10 in good shape, and Michael Paquier committed the counter split refactoring and the documentation of pg_stat_force_next_flush(). The main patch, now v18, gets only rebases with no new review since early September.
unclear: v1 could flush another backend by PID, and the material does not say whether dropping that, including for auxiliary processes, is final.
No benchmark covers many forced flushes in one transaction, where each flush walks all retained entries.
Bertrand's rule that custom callbacks must avoid cyclic dependencies does not appear as a documented contract in the material.
The thread does not say whether Michael accepts the main patch design, which was his suggested direction in the earlier thread.

prior_attempts.title: Flush some statistics within running transactions
prior_attempts.quote: This design requires enabling a new signal with a signal handler in a lot of processes that did not do that. Enabling timeouts in a bunch of new processes, while claiming it is fine to do, sounds like something we should rather be careful about.
prior_attempts.reason: Michael Paquier objected to the timeout design after the entry was marked Ready for Committer. He said it requires SIGALRM handlers and timeouts in many processes that never used them, and pgstat_schedule_anytime_update() calls in stats kinds and extensions. He proposed instead a procsignal-based client API (pg_stat_report()) with strategic flush calls, and opposed removing existing report calls. Sami Imseih's later idle-in-transaction timeout design did not help a single long analytical query, so no design reached agreement.
prior_attempts.what_is_different: P1 used a periodic timeout and later a stats_flush_interval GUC across backends and auxiliary processes. This proposal has no timer, no new signal handler and no GUC: the calling backend flushes on demand, which is the direction the P1 objector suggested according to message #1.

objections.title: Custom stats callbacks can silently double count after the API change
objections.failure_scenario: An extension with a custom variable-numbered kind is ported by adding the xact_boundary argument and returning PGSTAT_FLUSH_DONE. When a user calls pg_stat_force_next_flush() inside a transaction, the retained pending entry is merged again at the next flush or at commit. The inflated counters reach shared memory and the stats file written at shutdown, and nothing reports an error.
objections.argument: The patch keeps pending entries allocated mid-transaction (message #4), so every callback must now clear or baseline what it published. The rule exists only as a comment on flush_pending_cb (message #12). The signature change makes the build fail, but the minimal port that fixes the build is the one that double counts. Message #3 reordered the enum to avoid silent misbehavior in callbacks, but the retained-pending rule has no such guard.
objections.author_must_show: What makes a ported custom callback that does not clear or baseline its pending data fail visibly, for example in an assert-enabled build, rather than double count?

critic.reasoning: Message #12 confirms the no-double-merge rule exists only as a comment on flush_pending_cb, and the proposal has no check that makes a violation fail. The test module shows the pattern, but a minimal port that returns PGSTAT_FLUSH_DONE still double counts without notice.

objections.title: Existing function and C API get new semantics under the old name
objections.failure_scenario: An extension or test harness already calls pgstat_force_next_flush() or pg_stat_force_next_flush() inside a transaction, from a hook or from a function, expecting only a deferred flush. After upgrade, the call runs every flush callback on the spot, takes shared stats locks, and can raise an ERROR there. The caller sees this only when it fails.
objections.argument: v1 added a separate pg_stat_report_anytime(). v2 moved the immediate flush into the existing function, whose name still says the flush happens at the next occasion (message #2). Michael documented the function as end-of-transaction and test-oriented in message #36, and v18 changes that documented contract in the same cycle. The function also changes from PARALLEL RESTRICTED to PARALLEL UNSAFE, which can change plans for queries that already call it.
objections.author_must_show: Why should the existing deferred-flush function take on immediate-flush semantics rather than a new function or an option, given current C and SQL callers?

critic.reasoning: The thread gives no reason for moving the immediate flush into a function whose name says "next", so the consistency question stands. The documented-contract point is weak: that text was added this cycle and message #36 expects to update it.

refuted.title: Unchanged custom stats kinds can double count after a mid-transaction flush
refuted.failure_scenario: An extension with a custom stats kind written for an older release is rebuilt against the new headers, and its old bool callback still compiles. A user calls pg_stat_force_next_flush() inside a transaction. The pending entry is now kept, so the callback merges the same pending data again at commit, and the extension's view reports inflated numbers with no error.
refuted.argument: The enum was reordered in message #4 so that LOCK_CONFLICT is 0 and keeps the old meaning of false. That makes an old callback that returns true keep working, which hides the contract change. The new rule that a callback must not merge retained pending data twice is only a header comment (message #12). Only the in-core callbacks and the test module were changed to clear or baseline their data, and nothing fails loudly for an extension that was not changed.
refuted.author_must_show: What makes an extension with an unchanged custom stats kind fail to build, or refuse mid-transaction flushes, instead of double counting without notice?

critic.reasoning: The patch changes flush_pending_cb to take a third argument and return an enum, so an old two-argument bool callback gets an incompatible-pointer-type diagnostic, an error by default in current GCC and Clang. The ported-callback case is covered by replication-ondisk-1.

refuted.title: New flush callback contract for custom stats kinds fails silently
refuted.failure_scenario: An extension author ports a custom stats kind to the new flush_pending_cb signature, returns PGSTAT_FLUSH_DONE as before and does not clear or baseline the pending data. Each in-transaction flush then publishes the same counts again. Users see inflated numbers in the extension's view, and nothing fails.
refuted.argument: The signature change fails loudly at compile time, but the rules that matter do not. Callbacks must not merge retained data twice, must not call pgstat_force_next_flush(), and, per message #9, must not form cyclic dependencies. Message #12 adds a code comment for the first two, and the material shows no documented rule for the third. Each of these is a correctness duty that every custom kind now carries, with no check that catches a mistake.
refuted.author_must_show: Can the pgstat core enforce the no-double-merge rule, for example by keeping the baseline itself, so a custom callback cannot get it wrong silently?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of replication-ondisk-1. Its extra point about calling pgstat_force_next_flush() from a callback is already guarded by pgStatFlushInProgress since message #12.

refuted.title: Every future relation counter needs a correct transactional classification
refuted.failure_scenario: A later patch adds a relation counter that depends on commit or abort, and puts it in the non-transactional group. Its value is then published mid-transaction and never rolled back on abort. Users find out when their counts drift from reality after aborted transactions.
refuted.argument: Relation, index and function stats now each carry a counts and flushed baseline with delta logic. Message #15 notes that adding a counter already requires updating the merge and baseline logic. The static asserts in the split refactoring catch padding, but not a counter placed in the wrong group or left out of the baseline update. A committer reviewing an unrelated stats patch would likely miss this.
refuted.author_must_show: What fails in the regression tests when a new counter is put in the wrong group or left out of the flushed baseline?

critic.reasoning: The scenario depends on a mistake in a future patch. The committed split puts transactional counters in their own struct, so a new counter needs an explicit choice of group that a reviewer can see.

refuted.title: Repeated in-transaction flushes rescan all retained entries
refuted.failure_scenario: A pg_stat_statements version flushes at statement boundaries, as the example in message #2 shows. A batch transaction runs thousands of statements over many tables, and each flush walks every retained pending entry. The cost grows with statements times touched objects, and users see it as slower long transactions after an extension upgrade.
refuted.argument: Message #11 points out that the walk is 1 + 2 + ... + N callbacks. The only benchmark, in message #30, measured the per-pass reset scan at transaction boundaries, not many forced flushes in one transaction. The author answers that the caller throttles, but the stated main consumer is an extension that every user of pg_stat_statements would get, so the cost would no longer be opt-in in practice.
refuted.author_must_show: What does a transaction with many statements over hundreds of relations cost when it forces a flush after every statement?

critic.reasoning: The example in message #2 is throttled to once every 10 seconds and is not part of the patch. Message #12 says pg_stat_statements flushes only in the backend that reads the view, so the per-statement flush scenario does not follow from the material.

refuted.title: Patch as posted does not let anyone see another session's long transaction
refuted.failure_scenario: A DBA watching a long batch transaction in pg_stat_user_tables still sees nothing until it commits, because only the batch session itself can force the flush. Meanwhile every custom stats extension must adapt to the new flush_pending_cb signature and the no-double-merge rule in the release that ships this.
refuted.argument: The brief's motivation is long transactions that stay invisible, but v1's flush-by-PID was dropped (message #2), so only the running backend can trigger a flush. The automatic statement-boundary flush that would help users is a nocfbot demo (messages #2, #12), not part of the patch. The named consumers are tests (message #36) and the pg_stat_statements scalability work, which flushes only in the backend reading the view (message #12). [P1] shows the visibility demand is real, but its summary notes that a later design did not help a single long analytical query.
refuted.author_must_show: Which users, other than tests and the pg_stat_statements series, would call this inside their own transaction, and when does the automatic flush follow?

precedents.title: Flush some statistics within running transactions

critic.reasoning: Message #1 presents the patch as an on-demand API, the direction Michael Paquier suggested, with pg_stat_statements as the named consumer. [P1] failed over its timeout design and shows that a second author wanted this visibility, so it does not support the objection.

touch_points.label: catalog changes
touch_points.reason: pg_proc.dat changes pg_stat_force_next_flush() to PARALLEL UNSAFE and needs a catversion bump.

touch_points.label: ABI / extension API
touch_points.reason: flush_pending_cb gets an xact_boundary argument and an enum return type; flush_static_cb gets a transaction-boundary flag.

touch_points.label: SQL-standard conflict or non-standard syntax
touch_points.reason: see objection standards-compat-2: Existing function and C API get new semantics under the old name

touch_points.label: planner behaviour change
touch_points.reason: The PARALLEL UNSAFE marking stops parallel plans for queries that call pg_stat_force_next_flush().

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: Relation, index and function stats keep a flushed baseline with delta logic, and custom kinds carry a new no-double-merge rule.

touch_points.label: performance on the hot path
touch_points.reason: The patch touches the pending-stats flush path that every backend runs at transaction end.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)

questions: What makes a ported custom callback that returns PGSTAT_FLUSH_DONE without clearing or baselining its pending data fail visibly, for example in an assert-enabled build?
Why does the existing pg_stat_force_next_flush() take on the immediate flush, instead of a new function or an option as in v1?
Where is the rule that custom flush callbacks must avoid cyclic dependencies documented for extension authors?
What does one transaction cost when it forces many flushes over hundreds of retained entries?
Is dropping the flush of another backend by PID, including auxiliary processes, final for this patch?

committability.owner_note: Michael Paquier committed the counter split and the documentation of pg_stat_force_next_flush() from this thread. The thread does not say whether he accepts the main patch design.
committability.liability: The owner signs for the retained-pending and baseline logic in relation, index and function stats, and for the changed callback contract of custom stats kinds, for as long as custom kinds exist.
committability.author_follow_up: The author has posted 18 versions, adopted review feedback, and keeps rebasing, most recently moving the entry to the next CommitFest on 2026-11-10.

priority.reason: The patch is a prerequisite for the pg_stat_statements scalability work and serves users and tests that want current numbers from a long transaction. The main patch is about 98 KiB across all pgstat kinds and has had no new review since early September, so it needs a committer's design decision on the two open points.

provisional_note: The code was not read. The retained-entry and baseline logic, the requeue of entries during a pass, and error safety of a flush inside a transaction could not be judged from the prose.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: Flush some statistics within running transactions
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch set adds a per-kind flush property and a periodic timeout, later controlled by a stats_flush_interval GUC, so that backends and auxiliary processes flush non-transactional stats such as WAL, IO and read-related relation counters during running transactions. It also removes some existing explicit flush calls that the timeout makes redundant.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Michael Paquier objected to the timeout design after the entry was marked Ready for Committer. He said it requires SIGALRM handlers and timeouts in many processes that never used them, and pgstat_schedule_anytime_update() calls in stats kinds and extensions. He proposed instead a procsignal-based client API (pg_stat_report()) with strategic flush calls, and opposed removing existing report calls. Sami Imseih's later idle-in-transaction timeout design did not help a single long analytical query, so no design reached agreement.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
This design requires enabling a new signal with a signal handler in a
lot of processes that did not do that.  Enabling timeouts in a bunch
of new processes, while claiming it is fine to do, sounds like
something we should rather be careful about.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert "Add redo LSN to pgstats files"
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert "Add redo LSN to pgstats files"
Reverted commit(s): Add redo LSN to pgstats files
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commit b860848232aa, that was added as a prerequisite for
the support of pgstats data flush across checkpoints, linking a pgstats
file to a specific checkpoint redo LSN.

As reported, this is proving to be currently problematic when going
through a pg_upgrade, that does direct manipulations of the control file
in the new cluster.  The LSN stored in the pgstats file is not able to
cope with any changes done in the control file by pg_upgrade yet,
causing the pgstats file to be discarded when starting the new cluster
after overriding its redo LSN (one is a `pg_resetwal -l` where the new
cluster's start LSN is bumped by a hardcoded value of 8 segments, see
copy_xact_xlog_xid).

The least painful path going forward is likely going to be a refactor of
the pgstats code so as it is possible to read and write some of its data
with some routines in src/common/, so as pg_upgrade or pg_resetwal are
able to update its data.  The main point is that we are going to need a
LSN in the stats file should we make it written at checkpoint time and
not only as part of a shutdown sequence.  It is too late to dive into
these details for v18, so let's revert the change, and let's try to
figure out all the details in the next release cycle.  The pgstats file
is currently only written as part of a shutdown sequence, and its
contents are still lost on crash, same as older releases.

Bump PGSTAT_FILE_FORMAT_ID.

precedents_retrieved.title: Flush pgstats file during checkpoints
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch writes the pgstats file during non-shutdown checkpoints and restart points and stores the checkpoint redo LSN in the file. At startup, including crash recovery, stats load when the redo LSN matches, so statistics survive a crash.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Heikki Linnakangas found that stats entries can leak into the pgstats file after a crash, for example for a relation created in an uncommitted transaction. Since 5891c7a8ed nothing garbage-collects such orphaned entries. He also found that two immediate shutdowns in a row log an incorrect redo LSN warning, because the stats file is not flushed at the end-of-recovery checkpoint. Michael Paquier said he would look at these, and the visible messages end there.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: There are various race conditions where a stats entry can be leaked in the pgstats file.

precedents_retrieved.title: transaction statistics of logical replication subscription
precedents_retrieved.summary: The thread first proposed counting failed transactions and their sizes in pg_stat_replication_slots, so that users could tell successful logical decoding from repeated failed attempts. By the last version, the patch instead added apply_commit_count and apply_rollback_count columns to pg_stat_subscription_stats.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Amit Kapila noted that pg_stat_database already shows committed and rolled-back transactions per database, so the new counters largely duplicate it, and he asked whether anyone saw value in them. Masahiko Sawada agreed that commit and rollback counts without transaction sizes no longer meet the original goal and have no concrete use case. The author then marked the entry Returned with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
But I’m concerned that adding only apply_commit_count
and apply_rollback_count ends up adding the duplicate statistics with
no concrete use cases.

precedents_retrieved.title: Fix inconsistency in reporting checkpointer stats
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch fixes a mismatch between the checkpoint log message and the checkpointer statistics view: the log counts SLRU page writes in SlruInternalWritePage() as written buffers, but the view counts only BufferSync() writes. Later versions count SLRU writes in a separate slru_written column in pg_stat_checkpointer and list them separately in the log message.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why the entry closed as Returned with feedback, because Fujii Masao pushed the final version on 2024-10-02. Earlier, in January 2024, Michael Paquier returned an older entry because the patch no longer applied and columns had moved from pg_stat_bgwriter to pg_stat_checkpointer.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Some of the columns of pg_stat_bgwriter have
been moved to a different view, aka pg_stat_checkpointer.

precedents_retrieved.title: Flush SLRU counters in checkpointer process
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch makes the checkpointer report SLRU statistics during normal operation instead of only at server shutdown. After review it moved the WAL and SLRU stats reports into pgstat_report_checkpointer(), so they also run from CheckpointWriteDelay().
precedents_retrieved.objection: The patch's new pg_stat_slru test failed on Windows CI in 031_recovery_conflict. The author traced this to a race on have_slrustats and said a more stable version would follow, but none was posted. The entry was then returned with feedback, which message #9 gives as a consensus to prioritise other patches because this one was not in good shape.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
There
are many patches to be reviewed and this one doesn't seem to be in the
best shape, so we have to prioritise.

precedents_retrieved.title: explain to report bucket and memory stats for TupleHashTable nodes
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds bucket counts and peak memory statistics to explain analyze output for nodes that use a TupleHashTable, such as HashAggregate, HashSetOp and Bitmap Heap Scan. It also splits memory accounting into separate contexts for the hashtable and the tuples.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The hash spill to disk commit (1f39bce02) already added most of the instrumentation, and the author asked whether the patch still served a purpose. Jeff Davis said the extra detail should go under VERBOSE or a new explain option. The patch then stayed Waiting on Author from March, and Daniel Gustafsson closed the entry when no new activity followed.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:

and skimming the thread there seems to be questions raised over the value
proposition.

precedents_retrieved.title: pgstattuple: add test for coverage
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds SQL statements to the pgstattuple regression tests to raise code coverage from 50.6% to 78.7%. The tests insert data and check full `select *` output from the pgstattuple functions.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The tests added a dependency from pgstattuple on the bloom module, which Tom Lane objected to. The expected output also depended on platform details and failed on 32-bit systems. The author said he would fix it, but no updated version was posted, so Andres Freund marked the entry returned with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: You definitely can't rely on such details not to change across platforms.

precedents_retrieved.title: Report checkpoint progress with pg_stat_progress_checkpoint
precedents_retrieved.objectors: Michael Paquier, Andres Freund, Julien Rouhaud
precedents_retrieved.summary: The thread started as a proposal to log checkpoint progress in the server log. After objections it became a pg_stat_progress_checkpoint view that reports the checkpoint phase, flags, start LSN, start time and per-phase counters.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The final close came because the author stopped responding after Andres Freund marked the patch waiting on author for a docs build failure and noted that the architectural feedback had not reached a conclusion. Earlier, Michael Paquier returned it because the view was too complex and carried fields of little use, such as next_flags, start LSN and most flag values. Julien Rouhaud objected that the view showed the initial checkpoint flags instead of how the checkpoint was behaving now. Andres Freund measured progress-update overhead in BufferSync() on large shared_buffers.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: There has been no updates on this thread for some time, so this has been switched as Returned with Feedback.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert GetTransactionSnapshot() to return historic snapshot during LR
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert GetTransactionSnapshot() to return historic snapshot during LR
Reverted commit(s): Don't allow GetTransactionSnapshot() in logical decoding
precedents_retrieved.objection:
Commit 1585ff7387 changed GetTransactionSnapshot() to throw an error
if it's called during logical decoding, instead of returning the
historic snapshot. I made that change for extra protection, because a
historic snapshot can only be used to access catalog tables while
GetTransactionSnapshot() is usually called when you're executing
arbitrary queries. You might get very subtle visibility problems if
you tried to use the historic snapshot for arbitrary queries.

There's no built-in code in PostgreSQL that calls
GetTransactionSnapshot() during logical decoding, but it turns out
that the pglogical extension does just that, to evaluate row filter
expressions. You would get weird results if the row filter runs
arbitrary queries, but it is sane as long as you don't access any
non-catalog tables. Even though there are no checks to enforce that in
pglogical, a typical row filter expression does not access any tables
and works fine. Accessing tables marked with the user_catalog_table =
true option is also OK.

To fix pglogical with row filters, and any other extensions that might
do similar things, revert GetTransactionSnapshot() to return a
historic snapshot during logical decoding.

To try to still catch the unsafe usage of historic snapshots, add
checks in heap_beginscan() and index_beginscan() to complain if you
try to use a historic snapshot to scan a non-catalog table. We're very
close to the version 18 release however, so add those new checks only
in master.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert support for improved tracking of nested queries
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert support for improved tracking of nested queries
Reverted commit(s): Track more precisely query locations for nested statements; Fix regression with location calculation of nested statements; pg_stat_statements: Add tests for nested queries with level tracking
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This commit reverts the two following commits:
- 499edb09741b, track more precisely query locations for nested
statements.
- 06450c7b8c70, a follow-up fix of 499edb09741b with query locations.
The test introduced in this commit is not reverted.  This is proving
useful to track a problem that only pgaudit was able to detect.

These prove to have issues with the tracking of SELECT statements, when
these use multiple parenthesis which is something supported by the
grammar.  Incorrect location and lengths are causing pg_stat_statements
to become confused, failing its job in query normalization with
potential out-of-bound writes because the location and the length may
not match with what can be handled.  A lot of the query patterns
discussed when this issue was reported have no test coverage in the main
regression test suite, or the recovery test 027_stream_regress.pl would
have caught the problems as pg_stat_statements is loaded by the node
running the regression tests.  A first step would be to improve the test
coverage to stress more the query normalization logic.

A different portion of this work was done in 45e0ba30fc40, with the
addition of tests for nested queries.  These can be left in the tree.
They are useful to track the way inner queries are currently tracked by
PGSS with non-top-level entries, and will be useful when reconsidering
in the future the work reverted here.

roaster_notes.note: The one close precedent, [P1], died on its timeout and signal design, and this proposal drops both; v1's signal-by-PID path is gone too. Michael Paquier committed the prerequisite refactoring and the documentation patch (messages #40, #39), so the old reason does not carry over. Two points stay open for other angles. One is whether a self-only flush serves sessions watching a long transaction from outside. The other is whether the statement-boundary follow-up in message #2 brings back P1's timing questions.
pg_dump, psql and GUC concerns do not apply. The change of last_seq_scan and last_idx_scan to statement start time is documented and has a small effect, so it is not raised here.

The proposal changes no on-disk format, WAL, replication or wire protocol. The catalog change is a proparallel flip with a catversion bump. The only cross-boundary concern is the custom stats callback contract.

The current design flushes only the calling backend's own pending statistics into views that are already visible, so it gives no new access to other sessions or data. Cross-backend flushing by PID was dropped after v1. The material does not show whether pg_stat_force_next_flush() is granted to PUBLIC. It also has no measurement of a looped in-transaction flush contending on shared stats entry locks, but no concrete harm beyond what repeated short transactions already allow.
The goal is useful, a committer helped shape the design, and preparatory pieces are committed. The objections are about long-run contracts and cost, which a new version could address.

No existing feature gives other sessions a long transaction's counters before it ends. pg_stat_xact_* shows them only to the session that owns the transaction, and pg_stat_force_next_flush() waits for the transaction boundary. An extension cannot flush retained pending entries without core changes. The earlier attempt [P1] tried a timer-based design, and this proposal follows the on-demand API suggested there, so it does not duplicate an existing mechanism.
Demand for mid-transaction stats visibility is shown by [P1] and by Michael's test use (message #36). The objection concerns whether this step reaches those users.
